newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan issues appeal as oil hits bird sanctuaries.
newsitem.headline: Japan issues appeal as oil hits bird sanctuaries.

text.p: Japanese environment officials appealed on Tuesday for volunteers to clean up bird sanctuaries smeared with oil leaking from a sunken Russian tanker.

"Oil slicks have already hit the shores of Kanmurijima Island, 10 km (six miles) off the Kyoto region. The island is a summer nesting ground for 600,000 White-faced Shear Water birds," Environment Agency spokesman Tomo Mizutani said.
"We don't have the resources to clean up the slicks so it's down to volunteers," Mizutani told Reuters.

Mizutani said the seagull-like birds migrate only to Japan in the northern hemisphere, arriving on the 23-hectare (58-acre) island in February after spending the winter at feeding grounds in southern Asia.
"We also expect oil to arrive at Nanatsujima sanctuary, off the Noto Peninsula, where up to 6,000 Crested Murrelets, also a species unique to Japan, nest each year," he said.
Forecasts of bad weather added new urgency on Tuesday to efforts to clean up a 450-km (285-mile) stretch of coast on the Sea of Japan, about 320 km (200 miles) west of Tokyo.

The 13,157-tonne Nakhodka, a 26-year-old tanker carrying 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of heavy fuel oil from China to Russia, broke in two during stormy weather in early January, spilling much of its cargo and polluting rich fishing grounds and tourist beaches.
The 31-man crew of the tanker was rescued, but the captain is missing and presumed dead.
Maritime officials are concerned about continuing flows of oil from the stern of the Nakhodka, where two-thirds of the oil was stored. It went down about 115 km (70 miles) offshore.
The bow of the tanker, which has so far caused the most pollution, washed up on a rocky beach in the centre of the affected area a week ago.
The oil slick task force said it would drill holes in the beached bow section to drain off oil still in unruptured tanks.

The task force will try to syphon off the heavy oil through three holes drilled in the bow, thought to still contain over 2,000 tonnes of oil. It is grounded 100 metres (yards) offshore at Mikuni in Fukui Prefecture, a task force official said.
More than 40 patrol boats, seven helicopters, three planes and thousands of workers are involved in the cleanup of one of Japan's worst-ever oil spills.

"We're expecting the weather to get quite a bit worse... We are using as many ships as we can to carry out the cleanup near nuclear plants in Wakasa Bay, where fresh oil slicks are still arriving," a Maritime Safety Agency official said.

He said new slicks and solid clumps of oil were washing up along a ring of oil fences erected to protect 15 nuclear reactors scattered around Wakasa Bay, the world's greatest concentration of nuclear power plants.
A spokesman for Kansai Electric Co, which has 11 reactors in the bay region, said the fences had so far succeeded in keeping oil from intake pipes which provide vital cooling water to the reactors.
"There is no problem at the moment," the spokesman said.
The Transport Ministry said it would toughen checks on foreign vessels stopping at Japan's ports because of an increase in disasters at sea.
A ministry official said it would not be possible to check all foreign vessels calling at Japan's ports, but the inspections would be more thorough.
"We may take further measures to toughen checks due to the oil spill from the Russian tanker," the official said.
